newsitem.title: ITALY: Kosovo Albanians drop doubts on deal with Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Kosovo Albanians drop doubts on deal with Serbia.

text.p: The leader of ethnic Albanians in the troubled province of Kosovo has dropped late objections to a landmark deal with Serbia, the Roman Catholic peace group which brokered the accord said on Tuesday.
The Rome-based Sant'Egidio Community said the accord, which will allow Albanian students to return to Serbia's mainstream education system after a six-year boycott, was now fully agreed.
"It is done. It is a grand achievement," Mario Marazziti, the community's spokesman, told Reuters.
He said members of the group had met Ibrahim Rugova, leader of the opposition Albanian Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK), in the provincial capital Pristina on Monday night to resolve his objections.
Rugova and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic had signed separate copies of the accord in Belgrade and Pristina but Rugova then objected that the document did not refer explicity to universities.
"He (Rugova) came round to realise the success he had achieved," Marazziti said. He said Sant'Egidio would give more details of the agreement at a news conference later on Tuesday (1300 GMT).
According to Marazziti, the agreement is intended to have immediate effect, and will apply to all levels of education.
Western diplomats have praised the accord as a significant and welcome breakthrough in the Kosovo dispute, which has threatened to trigger a new Balkan war.
Tensions between ethnic Albanians, who outnumber Serbs nine to one in Kosovo, and Belgrade are considered the most potentially explosive unresolved ethnic conflict in the region.

The Albanian boycott of the Serbian education system began in 1990 in protest at Belgrade's move to revoke Kosovo's autonomous status a year earlier. The Albanians instead set up their own parallel education system for some 500,000 students and established an unofficial administration.

The United States and Germany have led diplomatic pressure on Belgrade to settle its differences with the Albanian leadership, before a so-called "outer wall" of economic sanctions against rump Yugoslavia can be lifted.
Sporadic violence has flared in recent months in Kosovo, which Serbs regard as the cradle of their civilisation, with a series of attacks on Serbian policemen.
International human rights groups accuse Serbia of using police-state methods to repress Albanians and protect Serbs.
